title: Password Security for Seniors: Simple Steps to Stay Safe Online
excerpt: Older adults are targeted by online scammers at disproportionate rates. This straightforward guide explains password security and account protection without technical jargon.
content:
Why Seniors Are Targeted — And What You Can Do About It

The FBI's Internet Crime Complaint Center consistently reports that adults over 60 lose more money to online fraud than any other age group — over $3 billion annually. This isn't because older adults are less intelligent. It's because scammers specifically design their attacks to exploit trust, authority, and urgency — tactics that work on everyone, but are particularly carefully crafted for older victims.

The good news: a few concrete habits make the vast majority of these attacks fail. This guide covers them clearly, without technical jargon.

The One Rule That Prevents Most Problems

If you take nothing else from this article, take this: never give anyone your password, and never give out a code that arrives by text or email to someone who called you.

Legitimate banks, government agencies, Microsoft, Apple, and Amazon will never call you and ask for your password or a verification code. If someone calls claiming there's an emergency with your account and you need to act right now — hang up. Then call the organization back using a number you find yourself (on their official website or the back of your card). The urgency is manufactured to stop you from thinking clearly.

Create Passwords You Don't Have to Memorize

A strong password for an online account doesn't need to be memorized — it needs to be stored securely. For most accounts, the best approach is to let a password manager generate and remember your passwords. Think of it like a locked address book for your passwords that only you can open.

If you prefer something you can look up yourself, the most secure option is a written list kept somewhere physically safe — not next to your computer, but in a drawer, a safe, or mixed in with other papers. This is genuinely more secure than reusing simple passwords, as long as you don't lose the list and don't share it.

For creating new passwords for your most important accounts, use our password generator — set it to 20 characters with all options checked, generate a password, and write it down before moving on.

The Three Most Important Accounts to Protect

You have many online accounts, but these three deserve your most urgent attention:

  1. Your email. This is the most critical. Anyone who gets into your email can reset every other password you have. Use a strong, unique password and turn on two-step verification (see below).
  2. Your bank and financial accounts. Use a strong, unique password. Set up text or email alerts for any transaction over $1. Review statements weekly.
  3. Medicare, Social Security, and health portals. Identity thieves use these to file fraudulent claims. Enable two-step verification wherever offered.

Two-Step Verification: What It Is and How to Turn It On

Two-step verification means that after entering your password, you also enter a short code sent to your phone by text message. Even if a scammer gets your password, they can't log in without your phone.

Here's how to turn it on for email:

  • Gmail: Click your photo in the top-right corner → Manage your Google Account → Security tab → 2-Step Verification → click Get Started and follow the prompts.
  • Yahoo Mail: Account Security → Two-step verification → toggle it on.
  • Outlook: account.microsoft.com → Security → Two-step verification.

When it asks 'how would you like to receive the code?' — choose 'Text message to my phone.' It's not the most advanced option, but it's easy and stops the vast majority of attacks.

Common Scams Targeting Older Adults Online

  • Tech support scams: A popup says your computer has a virus and you must call a number immediately. Do not call. Real security warnings from Windows or Apple never include a phone number to call. If worried, restart your computer — that closes most fake popups.
  • Romance scams: Someone you've met online (never in person) builds a relationship over weeks or months, then asks for money due to an emergency. Never send money to someone you haven't met in person, regardless of how well you feel you know them.
  • Grandparent scams: A caller claims to be your grandchild in trouble and asks for bail money or gift cards. Hang up and call your grandchild directly on their known number before doing anything.
  • Prize and lottery scams: You've won something but need to pay a fee first. Legitimate lotteries don't require payment to claim prizes.

Recommended Tools

For anyone new to password managers, NordPass has one of the simplest and cleanest interfaces available, with a free plan and biometric login on phones. 1Password offers a family plan, which means a tech-savvy family member can help set up and manage accounts together.
